12. A seed gains fresh mass but loses dry mass before leaves appear. Which interpretation best fits both readings?
A. New organic matter must have increased
B. Water must have been lost
C. No metabolism occurred
D. Water uptake occurred while reserves were respired
items.canonical_answer:
1. A. Mitosis keeps the chromosome number, so each daughter nucleus has 20. Distractors: B halves the number, which is meiosis; C gives four nuclei, which is also meiosis; D doubles the number, which does not happen in either division.
2. C. The fusion of gamete nuclei is the defining event. Distractors: A is ovulation; B is pollination; D moves seeds after reproduction.
3. B. The stigma receives the pollen grains. Distractors: A protects the bud; C produces pollen; D does not receive pollen.
4. D. The LH surge is the usual trigger for ovulation. Distractors: A controls blood glucose; B prepares the body for action; C mainly maintains the uterus lining.
5. B. rr is a pair of alleles, which is a genotype. Distractors: A, C and D are observable features, which are phenotypes.
6. A. Leaf length has a range of measured values with intermediates. Distractors: B, C and D are separate categories.
7. C. The homozygous recessive partner can only pass on the recessive allele, so the unknown parent’s alleles show in the offspring. Distractors: Option A can also pass on the dominant allele, which hides the unknown parent’s alleles; option B does not fix the genotype of the partner; option D cannot breed, because a cross must be within one species.
8. D. Aa × Aa: both parents show the dominant phenotype but each carries the recessive allele a, so each can pass on a and give an aa offspring. Distractors: In options A and B at least one parent is AA and can pass on only the dominant allele; option C includes an aa parent, which shows the recessive phenotype.
9. A. 12/20 is 60%, whereas 18/40 is 45%. Distractors: B names the lower percentage; C confuses the count with the proportion; D uses the wrong denominator.
10. C. Roan gives Cᴿ or Cᵂ and white gives Cᵂ, so half the offspring are roan. Distractors: A ignores the Cᴿ gametes; B belongs to a different cross; D ignores the white offspring.
11. B. Existing variation and predation cause unequal reproduction, so dark variants leave more offspring. Distractors: A says individuals choose to change; C says mutations are directed; D denies the unequal reproductive success that natural selection depends on.
12. D. Water increases the fresh mass while respiration uses up the stored food. Distractors: A contradicts the loss of dry mass; B contradicts the gain in fresh mass; C ignores the use of reserves.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for each question for choosing the correct option, 12 marks in total.
The answer key gives the correct option and says why each distractor is wrong.

items.prompt:
A learner investigated the effect of temperature on the germination of seeds. At each temperature she set up two separate samples of ten seeds taken from one batch. After five days she counted the seeds that had germinated, where germination means that a root at least 2 mm long has emerged. Her results are shown in the table. Describe and explain the results by answering parts (a) to (g).

| Temperature / °C | Germinated out of 10, sample 1 | Germinated out of 10, sample 2 | Mean germination / % |
|---|---|---|---|
| 15 | 3 | 4 | 35 |
| 20 | 8 | 9 | ... |
| 25 | 10 | 9 | 95 |
| 35 | 4 | 5 | 45 |

(a) State the independent variable. [1]
(b) State what was counted and the rule used to decide whether a seed had germinated. [1]
(c) Calculate the missing mean percentage at 20 °C. Show your working. [2]
(d) Describe the pattern in the results and identify the temperature with the highest germination. [2]
(e) State one variable, other than temperature, that should be kept the same. [1]
(f) Some samples at 35 °C dried out. Suggest why this is an error, and an improvement. [2]
(g) Suggest why 25 °C cannot be called the best temperature for germination from these results. [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Temperature.
(b) The number of seeds with an emerged root at least 2 mm long after five days.
(c) 8 + 9 = 17; 17 ÷ 20 = 0.85; 0.85 × 100 = 85, giving 85%.
(d) Germination increases from 15 °C to 25 °C, then falls at 35 °C; 25 °C gives the highest germination, 95%.
(e) Any one, such as the volume of water (moisture) or the light; the same seed batch or the same time is also accepted.
(f) Drying changes the water supply as well as the temperature, so the fall at 35 °C may be partly caused by lack of water. Check the dishes and add water to keep the moisture equal, without waterlogging.
(g) Temperatures between those tested, such as 30 °C, were not tested, so the best temperature could lie between them.
marking_guidance: (a) 1 mark for naming temperature as the variable that was changed. (b) 1 mark for the number of seeds germinated together with the 2 mm root rule.
(c) 1 mark for the method from the table data: (8 + 9) ÷ 20 × 100.
1 mark for the answer 85%. (d) 1 mark for the trend: germination rises up to 25 °C, then falls at 35 °C.
1 mark for identifying 25 °C as the temperature with the highest germination.
(e) 1 mark for one controlled variable, such as moisture or light. (f) 1 mark for the error: drying changes the water supply as well as the temperature.
1 mark for the improvement: keep the moisture equal in every dish.
(g) 1 mark for the limitation: temperatures between those tested, such as 30 °C, were not tested. The total is 10 marks.
